entities.name: John Hobart, 2nd Earl of Buckinghamshire
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John Hobart, 2nd Earl of Buckinghamshire (died 1793), was a prominent British statesman and diplomat whose career spanned critical junctures of the mid-to-late 18th century, profoundly influencing Anglo-Russian relations and grappling with escalating demands for legislative autonomy in Ireland. Succeeding his father, the 1st Earl, in 1756, Hobart ascended through the Whig political establishment, serving as a Lord of the Bedchamber to George II before embarking on a significant diplomatic posting that placed him at the heart of European power dynamics.

From 1762 to 1765, Hobart served as Ambassador to Russia, navigating the intricate court of Catherine the Great in the nascent years of her reign following the coup that deposed Peter III. His mission focused on securing a defensive alliance and fostering commercial ties, though he ultimately failed to achieve a formal treaty, partly due to Russian focus on Poland and the Ottoman Empire. Later, as Lord Lieutenant of Ireland from 1777 to 1780, during the tumultuous American Revolutionary War, he faced immense pressure from the Irish Patriot Party, led by figures like Henry Grattan, demanding legislative independence and free trade. His administration saw the rise of the Irish Volunteers, a paramilitary force initially formed for defense against French invasion, which quickly became a potent political instrument advocating for greater Irish autonomy.
